title: Affect in Peer Group Learning During Virtual Science Inquiry: Insights From Self-Reports and Video Observations
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how affect is expressed and experienced during collaborative science inquiry in a computer-based virtual learning environment, and whether affect is related to group performance. The authors ask whether students’ positive and negative emotions differ across phases of inquiry, whether affect differs by group outcome, and how self-reported affect compares with observed affect from video coding.

The intervention/context is a web-based virtual science inquiry environment called Virtual Baltic Sea Explorer (ViBSE). High school students worked in small peer groups on an interdisciplinary science task involving hypotheses, planning, experimentation in a virtual laboratory, analysis, and preparing a group presentation. Students completed repeated self-report affect scales after each working session, and researchers coded affective behavior from video segments using a multimethod approach.

The study included six carefully selected intact groups of three students each (18 students total) from a larger sample of 39 groups in Finnish high schools. The paper finds that positive affect was dominant overall in both self-reports and observations across all phases, though experimentation elicited relatively more negative affect. Differences between high-, average-, and low-performing groups were visible, especially in self-reports, but the authors report no clear effect of affect on group outcome. Observations generally showed lower-intensity affect than self-reports and revealed some negative affect that students did not report, underscoring the value of combining methods when studying collaborative science learning.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/multimethod observational study, not an RCT or QED. It provides rich descriptive evidence but does not meet higher-credibility causal criteria for intervention effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measurable positive impact of the virtual inquiry environment on outcome and includes no effect size. Findings are informative for design and affect in collaborative science learning, but the impact on learner outcomes is unclear and likely modest at best.

interventions.use_case: web-based virtual science inquiry environment (Virtual Baltic Sea Explorer) with simulation-based laboratory tasks for high school students investigating pH effects on copepods in the Baltic Sea food chain

finding.finding_summary: This study did not test an instructional improvement in science reasoning; instead, it examined whether affect related to group outcome during virtual science inquiry. Across six groups (n=18 focal students; 39 groups in the broader class), no effect of affect on group outcome was found, despite differences in presentation quality across high, average, and low groups.
finding.measure: quality of final group presentation in a virtual science inquiry task (research plan, hypotheses, understanding, presentation structure, conclusions, scientific language)
finding.study_size: n=18 focal students (6 groups); broader class n=120, 39 groups

finding.finding_summary: Positive affect was prevalent across self-reports and observations, but the Experimentation phase showed more negative affect than the other phases in self-reports (e.g., 33% negative vs. 12% in Planning and 10% in Conclusions). Across groups, high-performing groups were more consistently positive, while low-performing groups showed more negative affect; however, the study concluded that affect did not predict group outcome overall.
finding.measure: self-reported affect scale and video-coded observed affect (valence and arousal/intensity) across planning, experimentation, and conclusions phases

finding.finding_summary: The paper closely examined collaborative interaction and within-group consistency in affect during joint science inquiry. High-performing groups showed more consistent positive affect and smoother collaboration, whereas the average and low groups showed more ambivalence, confusion, and unequal participation; no numeric effect size was reported.
finding.measure: video-observed interaction quality, within-group affect consistency, and participation patterns during collaborative inquiry
